title: How to Avoid Tragedy: Study Tragedy
author: Matt Spivey
summary: Prompted by the death of academic Jason Arday amid a fraud scandal, Spivey, a former college literature instructor, argues that Arday's downfall follows the exact structure of classical tragedy that humanities education is supposed to teach: a talented, admired figure whose unchecked ambition and manufactured identity collapse under their own weight, exactly as dramatized in Oedipus Rex, The Scarlet Letter, and Crime and Punishment. He draws the Oedipus parallel in detail, a man of high status and intelligence who investigates his own myth-making past against warning, ultimately discovering he is the source of the very plague he claims to be fighting, and argues that if Arday's teachers had emphasized these artistic myths of Western civilization over fawning over his constructed identities and empty pedagogies, his path might have been different. Spivey's broader claim is that tragic literature exists precisely to offer readers a way out, or at least a way through, before catastrophe, a function he argues contemporary humanities education has abandoned. The piece functions as both a eulogy-adjacent cultural commentary and an argument for the classical position that humanities education exists to help people survive by internalizing the accumulated moral lessons of the past.
points: Spivey's central argument is structural, not merely thematic: he maps Arday's actual biographical arc onto Oedipus Rex point-for-point to argue tragedy's warnings are literal, not just symbolic.

He locates the failure in pedagogy rather than in Arday alone, arguing his teachers should have taught the classic literary studies of deception and ambition instead of fawning over his constructed identities.

The essay's defining claim about tragedy's function, that classical tragic works include a Tiresias-like figure offering a way out before the fall, reframes the genre as preventive moral instruction rather than mere catharsis.

Spivey closes by tying the argument to his broader thesis that the purpose of education is to help us survive, positioning classical literary study as practically protective rather than merely aesthetic or historical.
quotes: How many pieces of literature have shown us the dangers of masking one's identity, overvaluing ambition and status, using words and power to manipulate others, and collapsing under the weight of revealed reality?

Oedipus is a man of high status who has a complicated background. He is held in high regard for his intelligence, adored across the land. And he claims to bring peace and opportunity to a downtrodden people.
Oedipus, after fighting against a plague, comes to realize he is the plague. He has brought about his own downfall.
The blindness, the obsession with status, the unrelenting adherence to a fated fall, they stuck to their stories, when letting go might have saved them.

But many of the famous tragic works of literature from our culture had a character offering a way out, or at least a way through. There are teachers and advisors offering wisdom, clowns and choruses acting as consciences, hinting at ways the stars of our stories might take a closer look at themselves.
As I wrote in a long essay a few weeks ago, the purpose of education is to help us survive. The humanities, specifically, do that by teaching us to remember the lessons of the past.
